title: How animals talk: the messages in barks, purrs and birdsong

summary.text: A dog barks one way at a stranger and another way when she wants to play. Animals send each other messages with sounds, with their bodies and with touch. A sound or movement that carries a message to another animal is called a signal. Your child sends four messages using only the made-up word 'la-la', from behind a door, and finds out whether the tune of a sound can carry a message with no words at all.
summary.art: A brown street dog with one white ear barking at a building gate, while a girl on a balcony above listens with her hand cupped behind her ear.

intro.hook: A dog is barking at the gate downstairs. You cannot see the dog. Is the dog saying 'go away', 'let's play' or 'I am lonely'? How could you tell, just by listening?
intro.text: Animals talk to each other all day. Dogs bark and growl. Cats purr and hiss. Crows caw, koels call and crickets chirp at night. Each sound is a message for someone. In this unit you listen to animal sounds and find out what they mean. Then you test whether a message can get through with no words at all.
intro.art: A city flat window at evening with speech-bubble shapes coming from a crow on the ledge, a dog at the gate below and a cricket in a potted plant.

outcomes: By the end I can say what communicating means: one animal sends a message, and another animal notices and changes what they do.
By the end I can name three ways animals send messages: with sounds, with their bodies and with touch.
By the end I can say how a cat purrs, and that a purr does not always mean 'I am happy'.
By the end I can tell a bird's song from a bird's call, and say what each one is for.
By the end I can say that low, rough sounds often mean 'stay away', and high, soft sounds often mean 'I am friendly' or 'help me'.
By the end I can test whether a message gets through from the tune of a sound alone, and say what I found.

terms.meaning: To communicate is to send a message to someone else, who notices it and acts on it.
terms.example: A mother hen clucks, and her chicks run to her. She has communicated with them.
terms.art: A hen clucking with her beak open and five yellow chicks running towards her.

terms.meaning: A signal is a sound, a movement, a touch or a smell that carries a message.
terms.example: A cat walking towards you with her tail straight up is giving a signal. It usually means 'hello, I am friendly'.
terms.art: A grey cat walking towards the viewer with her tail held straight up like a flagpole.

terms.meaning: A call is a short animal sound with one message, such as 'danger', 'food here' or 'where are you?'.
terms.example: A crow gives a loud, harsh caw when a cat walks below the tree.
terms.art: A house crow on a branch, beak wide open, looking down at a cat on a wall.

terms.meaning: A song is a long pattern of sounds that a bird repeats, often to say 'this is my place' or to attract a partner.
terms.example: A magpie robin sings a long, sweet song from the top of a water tank early in the morning.
terms.art: A black and white magpie robin singing on the edge of a rooftop water tank at sunrise.

terms.meaning: An alarm call is a call that warns others that danger is near.
terms.example: When a cat comes close, a squirrel on a tree gives a fast 'chip-chip-chip' and flicks her tail.
terms.art: A palm squirrel with three stripes on a tree trunk, tail flicked up, looking down at a cat.

terms.meaning: A purr is the soft, buzzing rumble a cat makes with her voice box, breathing in and breathing out.
terms.example: A cat curled up on your lap purrs, and you can feel the buzz in your legs.
terms.art: A grey cat curled on a child's lap with small wavy lines around her body to show the purr.

terms.meaning: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. A whistle has a high pitch. A big drum has a low pitch.
terms.example: A puppy's whine has a high pitch. A big dog's growl has a low pitch.
terms.art: A small puppy with a thin high wavy line coming from the mouth, next to a big dog with a thick low wavy line.

terms.meaning: To vibrate is to shake back and forth very fast. Every sound is made by something vibrating.
terms.example: Put your fingers on your throat and hum. You can feel your voice box vibrate.
terms.art: A child's fingers resting on the front of their throat while they hum, with small buzz lines.

explanations.context: This card says what scientists mean when they say animals communicate.
explanations.definition: Communicating is sending a signal that another being notices and acts on.
explanations.description: Every message needs two: a sender and a receiver. The sender gives a signal. The signal can be a sound, a movement, a touch or a smell. The receiver notices the signal and does something because of it. A crow caws at a cat, and the other crows fly up. A hen clucks, and her chicks come running. Humans are animals too, and we communicate with words, faces, hands and the tune of our voice.
examples: A street dog barks at a stranger, and the watchman comes to the gate.
Two ants meet and touch antennae, then one turns round and follows the other's path.
A baby cries, and her mother picks her up.
explanations.art: Two crows on a wire: one cawing with an open beak at a cat below, the other already lifting off, with an arrow from the first crow to the second.

explanations.concept: How birds talk: songs and calls
explanations.context: This card is about the two kinds of sounds birds make.
explanations.definition: A bird's call is short and carries one message. A bird's song is longer, is repeated again and again, and often says 'this is my place' or 'choose me'.
explanations.description: Calls are for everyday messages: 'danger', 'I am here', 'feed me'. Songs are longer, and many songbirds learn them by listening to grown-up birds, the way you learned to talk. People once thought only male birds sing. In 2014 a team led by Karan Odom checked over a thousand kinds of songbirds. In most of the kinds that they could check, the females sing too.
examples: A male koel calls 'ku-oo, ku-oo', higher each time, again and again in the hot months. A female koel has her own sharp 'kik-kik-kik' call.
A magpie robin sings a long, sweet song from a rooftop at dawn.
A bulbul gives a sharp alarm call when a cat comes near the nest.
explanations.art: Two panels: a magpie robin singing a long wavy line of notes on a rooftop, and a bulbul giving one short sharp spike of sound at a cat.

explanations.context: This card is about how one dog sound can carry many messages.
explanations.definition: A bark is a short, loud sound a dog makes to send a message. Dogs bark in different ways in different situations.
explanations.description: When a stranger comes, a dog's barks are often low, rough and fast, with no gaps. When a dog wants to play, the barks are often higher, with gaps between them. A dog left alone may give high barks and whines. In 2005 Péter Pongrácz and his team in Hungary played recordings of dog barks to people. Most people could tell the situations apart better than by chance, even people who had never owned a dog.
examples: Low, rough, fast barks at the gate: 'A stranger is here. Stay back.'
Higher barks with gaps, and a play bow: 'Let's play!'
A growl over a bowl of food: 'This is mine. Do not come closer.'
explanations.art: Three small pictures of the same brown dog: barking hard at a gate, doing a play bow with a ball, and growling over a food bowl.

explanations.context: This card is about the purr, and why scientists still argue about it.
explanations.description: A cat purrs with her voice box, the part of the throat that makes sounds. The purr goes on while she breathes in and while she breathes out. Her voice box shakes more than 20 times every second, so you can feel the buzz. Cats purr when they are calm and close to someone. They also purr when they are hungry, hurt or giving birth. So a purr does not always mean 'I am happy'.
examples: A cat purrs on a lap, with eyes half shut.
A mother cat purrs while her kittens drink her milk.
A cat with a hurt paw purrs at the vet.

perspectives.explanation: A purr often means 'stay close' or 'I am calm with you'. A mother's purr may help her kittens find her, because they are born with their eyes and ears shut and can feel the buzz.

perspectives.who: Karen McComb and her team, in England (2009)
perspectives.explanation: When some cats purr for food, they hide a high cry inside the purr. People find this purr harder to ignore. So a purr can also be a way of asking.
A cat may purr when hurt to calm herself. Some think the buzz may even help the body heal. This idea has not been shown yet.

explanations.art: A grey cat purring on a lap, a mother cat purring with three kittens drinking milk, and a cat with a bandaged paw purring on a vet's table.

explanations.context: This card is about a pattern that scientists found in the sounds of many kinds of animals.
explanations.description: In 1977 Eugene Morton, a bird scientist in America, compared the sounds of many birds and mammals. Low, rough sounds often mean 'stay away'. High, soft, clear sounds often mean 'I am friendly', 'I am scared' or 'help me'. A big body makes a deeper sound, so a low growl makes an animal sound bigger. In 2017 Piera Filippi and her team played sounds of frogs, alligators, pandas and elephants to people, and most people could hear whether the animal was calm or excited. This is a pattern with exceptions, not a rule for every sound.
examples: A dog growls low over a bone. A puppy whines high when left alone.
A cat hisses with a rough sound when a strange dog comes near.
People speak low and rough when they are angry, and high and soft to a baby.
explanations.art: A row of animals, a dog, a cat, a crow and a girl, each shown twice: once with a thick low jagged sound line and a cross face, once with a thin high smooth line and a soft face.

explanations.context: This card is about messages that animals send with their bodies, their wings and touch.
explanations.definition: Many signals are not made with a voice at all. Animals send messages with how they hold their bodies, with sounds made by other body parts, and with touch.
explanations.description: A cat with her tail straight up is saying hello. A cat with puffed-up fur and an arched back is saying 'stay away'. A dog does a play bow, front legs down and back end up, to say 'this is a game'. A male cricket chirps by rubbing one wing against the other, and female crickets hear him with ears on their front legs. In 2020 Tasmin Humphrey and Karen McComb found that cats often blink slowly back when a person slow-blinks at them.
examples: A dog doing a play bow, tail waving.
A cricket rubbing his wings together in a potted plant at night.
A cat slowly closing and opening her eyes at you from across the room.
explanations.art: A dog in a play bow, a cat with tail straight up, and a cricket on a leaf with wings lifted, each with a small label of their message.

agreed.text: Many animals send messages with sounds, body movements, touch and smell, and other animals act on them.
agreed.evidence: Scientists record a signal, then play it back with a hidden speaker when nothing else is happening. If animals act on the sound alone, the sound carries a message. Tests like this have been done with monkeys, birds, frogs, crickets and many more.

agreed.text: Cats purr with their voice box, and the purr goes on while they breathe in and out.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured the voice box and breathing of purring cats. The buzz carries on through both breaths, which is why a purr sounds unbroken.

agreed.text: Many songbirds learn their songs by listening to grown-up birds.
agreed.evidence: In the 1950s William Thorpe raised young chaffinches who never heard a grown-up sing. They grew up singing a much plainer song than wild chaffinches.

challenging.who: A common idea in many old bird books, written mostly in Europe and North America, where in many kinds of birds mostly males sing.
challenging.for: In many birds near those scientists' homes, the males sang far more than the females.
challenging.against: In 2014, a team led by Karan Odom checked over a thousand kinds of songbirds around the world. In most of the kinds they could check, females sing too. In many tropical birds, a female and male even sing a duet together.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea that left out half the birds.

challenging.claim: A wagging tail always means a dog is happy and friendly.
challenging.for: Happy, friendly dogs often wag their tails loosely, with the whole back end swinging.
challenging.against: Dogs also wag when they are excited, unsure or ready to snap. A stiff tail held high, wagging fast in small movements, can be a warning. You have to look at the whole dog: ears, mouth, body and tail.
challenging.context: This card is about reading a dog's tail.

challenging.claim: A purring cat is always a happy cat.
challenging.for: Cats often purr when they are calm, warm and close to someone they trust.
challenging.against: Cats also purr when they are hurt, hungry, frightened or giving birth. Vets often hear cats purr on the table.
challenging.context: This card is about what a purr means.

challenging.who: Many scientists who study language, such as Noam Chomsky
challenging.for: Humans put words together to say endless new things, even things that are far away or did not happen. No other animal has been shown to do this the way we do.
challenging.against: Vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and other vervets act on each call in its own way. Some birds and monkeys put calls together in a set order. Scientists are still finding out how much other animals can say.
challenging.context: This card is about whether animal calls are a kind of language.

big_questions.q: A cat purrs when she is happy and also when she is hurt. How could another cat, or you, know which one she means?
big_questions.hint: Think about what else you can see and hear: her eyes, her ears, her body, and what just happened.

big_questions.q: Why might a 'go away' sound be low and rough in so many different animals?
big_questions.hint: Think about who makes deep sounds: a big drum or a small one, a big dog or a puppy.

big_questions.q: When you talk to a dog, what does the dog understand: your words, or the tune of your voice?
big_questions.hint: Try saying 'good dog' in a cross voice, and 'bad dog' in a happy voice, and watch what the dog does.

big_questions.q: Do animals have words, or are their sounds only feelings coming out?
big_questions.hint: Remember the vervet monkeys, with different calls for a leopard, an eagle and a snake.

big_questions.q: If we could understand every animal around our home, what do you think they would be saying?
big_questions.hint: Think about the crows, the pigeons, the street dogs and the geckos, and what each of them needs.

story.title: The Bark at the Gate
story.note: Kavya, Rohan, Shanthi Atthe, Fathima Aunty, Rani and Bekku are made up. These facts are real: dogs often bark low and fast at strangers and higher, with gaps, in play, dogs use a play bow to start a game, cats purr when calm and also when hurt, and male and female koels have different calls.
text: Kavya lived on the second floor of a flat in Mysuru. She was seven. Her little brother Rohan was five. Their aunt, Shanthi Atthe, was a vet. She looked after sick animals at a shelter near the lake.
A street dog called Rani slept by the gate of their building. Rani was brown, with one white ear. Every morning, the watchman's wife gave her a bowl of rice and curd.
One Saturday morning, Rani began to bark. "Woof! Woof! Woof!" The barks were low, rough and fast, with no gaps. Kavya ran to the balcony. A man in a red shirt stood at the gate with a big parcel.
"Rani is angry," said Rohan. "She hates that man."

Shanthi Atthe came out with her cup of coffee. "Listen to the bark, not just the noise," she said. "Low, rough and fast. Rani has never seen this man. She is telling him, 'This is my place. Stay back.'"
The watchman came out. He spoke to the man and took the parcel. Rani stopped barking at once. She lay down again, with her nose on her paws.
"So the bark was for the watchman too?" asked Kavya.
"Maybe," said Atthe. "One bark can have many listeners."

That evening, Rohan went down to the gate with his ball. Rani jumped up. She put her front legs flat on the ground and kept her back end high. Her tail waved from side to side. Then she barked again. But these barks were higher, with gaps between them. "Woof! ... Woof! ..."
Rohan hid the ball behind his back. "Is she angry again?" he asked.
Kavya looked at Rani. She thought about the morning. "No," she said. "Listen. Her barks are higher and slower. And look at her. Her front legs are down and her tail is up. She wants to play."
Rohan threw the ball. Rani raced after it and brought it back, tail waving.
"That bow is called a play bow," said Atthe from the balcony. "Dogs use it to say, 'What comes next is a game.'"

On Sunday, Fathima Aunty from next door came to visit with her cat, Bekku. Bekku was grey, with a white chin. She climbed onto Kavya's lap and curled up. Soon a soft rumble came from her. Kavya could feel the buzz in her own legs.
"She is purring!" whispered Kavya. "She is happy."
"Often, yes," said Atthe. "When a cat purrs, her voice box shakes more than twenty times every second. That is why you can feel it."
A few weeks later, Bekku jumped off a wall and hurt her paw. Fathima Aunty carried her to the shelter. Bekku lay on Atthe's table, and she purred the whole time.
"Why is she purring?" asked Kavya. "She is hurt."

"Cats purr when they are hurt or frightened too," said Atthe. "Scientists still argue about why. One idea is that the purr helps to calm her. So a purr does not always mean 'I am happy'. You have to look at what is happening too."
Outside, a bird called from the neem tree. "Ku-oo! Ku-oo! Ku-oo!" Each call went higher than the one before.
"That is a male koel," said Atthe. "He calls again and again in the hot months. He is saying, 'I am here.'"
A little later came a different sound, sharp and bubbling. "Kik-kik-kik-kik!"
"And that is a female koel," said Atthe. "She has her own call."

That night, Kavya had an idea. She made four cards. The first said 'Go away!'. The second said 'I am happy'. The third said 'Help, I'm scared!'. The fourth said 'Come here!'. She took the cards behind the bedroom door.
"Rohan, I will only say 'la-la'," she called. "No other words. You guess which card I am holding."
She picked 'Go away!'. "La-la!" she said, low and rough, like Rani at the gate.
"Go away!" shouted Rohan at once.
She picked 'Help, I'm scared!'. "La-la?" she squeaked, high and shaky.
Rohan thought for a moment. "Scared?"
They played twelve times. Rohan got nine right. He mixed up 'I am happy' and 'Come here' twice, and missed 'scared' once.
Kavya came out from behind the door. "You knew what I meant, and I said no real words," she said. "My voice was low and rough when I said go away. Just like Rani's bark at the stranger."
Atthe smiled. "Many animals do the same," she said. "Dogs growl low. Cats hiss. People make their voices low and rough when they are angry. High, soft sounds often mean 'I am friendly' or 'help me'."
Rohan looked out of the window at the gate. Rani was asleep under the light. "Can Rani understand us, then?" he asked.
"She hears our tune," said Kavya. "Tomorrow, let's find out how much."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya learns that one kind of sound, a bark or a purr, can carry different messages, and that you read a message from its tune and from what is happening. In her la-la game she finds that a message gets through even with no real words.
ask: How did Kavya know that Rani's evening bark meant 'let's play'?
Why was Bekku purring on the vet's table?
In the la-la game, how did Rohan guess 'Go away!' with no words?
What do you think Kavya and Rohan will try with Rani tomorrow?

experiments.title: The La-La Test: can a message get through with no words?
experiments.context: In this experiment one person hides behind a door and sends four messages using only the made-up word 'la-la'. The listener cannot see them, and guesses each message from the sound alone.
experiments.question: Can a listener tell which message you are sending, from the tune of 'la-la' alone, with no words and no face to see?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Out of 12 tries, how many will your listener get right? Which message will be easiest to guess, and which will be hardest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The word is always 'la-la', so only the tune changes. The sender hides behind a door, so the face and hands cannot help. The slips are mixed in a bowl, so the listener cannot guess the order. Each message is sent 3 times, because one try can be luck.

materials.item: a bowl or a steel dabba to mix the slips in
a door that can be half shut, or a bedsheet hung over a chair
a notebook page for the results table

schedule.what: Make 12 message slips, guess, send 12 la-la messages from behind a door, then count which messages got through. If there is time, swap places and send 12 more.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw a tally for each message: how many times out of 3 the listener got it right. Circle the easiest message.

setup.art: Twelve paper slips on a table in four groups of three: an angry face with 'Go away!', a smiling face with 'I am happy', a scared face with 'Help, I'm scared!', and a waving hand with 'Come here!'.
setup.caption: 1. Make 12 slips: each of the 4 messages 3 times.

setup.art: The slips folded and mixed in a steel dabba, with a child's hand picking one out.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the slips and mix them in a bowl.

setup.art: A girl hidden behind a half-open door reading a slip, while her mother sits on the other side with her back to the door, listening.
setup.caption: 3. The sender hides and says 'la-la' the way the slip says.

setup.art: A notebook table with four columns and tick and cross marks, and a mother writing in it.
setup.caption: 4. The listener guesses. Write the guess and whether it was right.

flow.do: 1. Cut 12 small slips of paper. 2. On 3 slips, draw an angry face and write 'Go away!'. 3. On 3 slips, draw a smiling face and write 'I am happy'. 4. On 3 slips, draw a scared face and write 'Help, I'm scared!'. 5. On 3 slips, draw a waving hand and write 'Come here!'.
flow.say: Animals send messages without words. Let's see if we can do it too. We need four messages, and each one three times.
flow.kid: Make 12 slips. Draw the four messages. Make each one three times.
flow.parent: Your child can draw and you can write the words. The drawings help a child who is not reading yet.

flow.do: Ask your child for a guess and a reason before you start.
flow.say: You will only say 'la-la'. I will not see you. Out of 12 tries, how many will I guess right? Which message will be easiest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. How many will the listener get right? Which one is easiest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that message will be easiest?
good: 'Go away' is easy because I can make my voice cross.
'Scared' is easy because my voice goes high and wobbly.

flow.parent: Write the guess at the top of the page. Any guess is fine. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Fold all 12 slips and mix them in the bowl. 2. The sender takes the bowl behind the door. 3. The listener sits on the other side, back to the door.
flow.say: You are the sender first. Take the bowl behind the door. I will sit here and not look.
flow.kid: Take the bowl behind the door. Do not let the listener see you.
flow.parent: Hiding matters. If the listener can see a face, the face gives the answer away. Then we would not know what the sound alone can do.

flow.do: 1. The sender picks one slip and reads it silently. 2. The sender says 'la-la' once or twice, in the way the slip says. 3. The listener says their guess. 4. Write the slip, the guess, and right or wrong. 5. Put the slip aside. 6. Do all 12 slips.
flow.say: Pick a slip. Don't tell me what it says. Just say 'la-la' the way the message feels. I'll guess.
flow.kid: Pick a slip. Say only 'la-la'. Make it sound like the message.
flow.parent: Do not give hints, and do not say whether a guess was right until all 12 are done. A hint helps the next guess and makes the test unfair. If your child says a real word by mistake, put that slip back in the bowl.

flow.do: Optional, about 8 more minutes: swap. Now the parent hides and sends, and your child listens. Fold the slips and mix them again first. Do all 12 again, and write the results in a second table.
flow.say: If we have time, let's swap. I will hide, and you listen. Let's see if you can read my la-la.
flow.kid: Now you listen. Guess each message from the sound.
flow.parent: Swapping shows whether it was one good sender, or whether the tune works for anyone.

flow.do: 1. Count how many guesses were right in each table. 2. Make a tally for each message. 3. Ask how the 'Go away!' la-la sounded, and how the 'Help, I'm scared!' la-la sounded.
flow.say: How many did we get right? Which message got through best? When you said 'go away', was your voice high or low? Rough or smooth? And when you were scared?
flow.kid: Count the right guesses. Which message was easiest? Was 'go away' low or high?

ask.q: What did you hear that told you the message?
good: The 'go away' was low and loud and rough.
The scared one was high and shaky.
The happy one went up and down, like singing.

check.q: In the la-la test, the word was the same every time. What carried the message?
options: The tune of the voice: high or low, rough or smooth, loud or soft
Nothing. The listener was only lucky
check.why: 'La-la' has no meaning, so the word could not help. The listener could not see the sender either. Only the tune changed, so the tune carried the message. If you picked luck, look at your table: with 4 messages, luck alone would give about 3 right out of 12.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what your child saw: 'I got 9 right. The go away one was low and rough, and I got it every time.' Now read the card 'The tune carries the message'. Messages that are often mixed up, like 'happy' and 'come here', are normal. Both are friendly sounds.

experiments.title: Do They Know Their Name? A test with a pet cat or dog (if you have one)
experiments.context: In this experiment you say four words that sound a little like a pet's name, and then the name itself. You watch whether the pet turns their ears or head more for their own name. Do it only with a pet cat or dog who lives with you or with a friend.
experiments.question: Does a pet cat or dog move more when they hear their own name than when they hear other words like it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the pet move their ears or head more for their name, or the same for every word? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every word is said in the same voice, at the same loudness, from the same place. The words have the same number of beats as the name. You wait the same time between words. The pet cannot see your face, so only the sound can help.

materials.item: a pet cat or dog who lives with you or with a friend, resting calmly
a clock or a phone timer to count 15 seconds

experiments.safety: Do this only with a pet who knows you, and only when they are calm. Never wake a sleeping animal or disturb one who is eating. Do not try it with a street dog you do not know.

schedule.what: Choose four words like the pet's name, say them one by one, then the name, and watch what the pet does each time. Repeat with a second person.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a tick or a cross for each word. Draw the pet the moment you said their name.

setup.art: A grey cat resting on a sofa, looking away, while a girl stands behind the sofa out of the cat's sight with a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Wait until the pet is calm and not looking at you.

setup.art: The same cat turning both ears and her head towards the girl, with a small speech bubble saying 'Bekku'.
setup.caption: 2. Say four other words, then the name. Watch the ears and head.

flow.do: 1. Choose four words with the same number of beats as the pet's name. For a cat called Bekku, as in the story, you might use 'pakku', 'tikku', 'mukku' and 'sakku'. 2. Write them in the table, with the name last.
flow.say: We will say four words that sound a bit like the pet's name. Then the real name. Which words shall we use?
flow.kid: Choose four words that sound like the pet's name. Write them down.
flow.parent: This test comes from Atsuko Saito and her team in Tokyo. In 2019 they found that many pet cats moved their ears and heads more for their own name than for similar words.

flow.do: Ask your child for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Will the pet move more for the name, or the same for every word? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the pet notice their name more? Why?

good: Yes, because we call the name when we give food.
No, because all the words sound the same.

flow.do: 1. Stand where the pet cannot see your face. 2. Say the first word in a normal voice. 3. Watch for 15 seconds. Did the ears move? Did the head turn? 4. Write ticks or crosses. 5. Do the same for words 2, 3 and 4. 6. Then say the name, the same way.
flow.say: Same voice every time. Now watch closely. Did the ears move? Did the head turn?
flow.kid: Watch the ears and the head. Tick what you see.
flow.parent: Ears can move very quickly. Watch the ears, not just the head. If the pet walks away, stop and try another day. A pet who comes to you is giving a big answer.

flow.do: Another day, or after an hour, let a different family member say the words and the name. Use the same words in the same order.
flow.say: Let's try with another voice. Does the pet notice their name from a different person too?
flow.kid: Let someone else say the words. Watch again.
flow.wait: Do this an hour later, or the next day, so the pet is calm again.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Did the pet move more for their name? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Did the pet notice their name most? What did you see?

ask.q: Why might a pet notice their name?
good: Because good things happen after the name, like food or a cuddle.
Because people say the name a lot.

check.q: Why did we say every word in the same voice?
options: So that only the word changed, and not the tune
So that the pet would fall asleep
Because pets only hear one voice
check.why: If you said the name in a happy voice and the other words in a flat voice, the pet might answer the happy tune, not the name. Keeping the voice the same makes the test fair.

flow.parent: Some pets show little difference, and that is a real result too. In Saito's test, not every cat answered. Talk about what else the pet might be noticing: your footsteps, the time of day, the smell of food.

activities.title: Hum a Purr: feel a sound in your throat
activities.context: In this activity you hum and feel your voice box vibrate, the way a cat's voice box vibrates when she purrs. Then you try to hum while breathing in, the way a cat purrs.

materials.item: a pet cat, if one lives with you (optional)

schedule.what: Hum low and high with fingers on the throat, try humming while breathing in, and feel a cat's purr if a cat is near.

activities.record: Draw your throat and the buzz you felt for a low hum and for a high hum. Write which one buzzed more.

setup.art: A child with two fingers resting gently on the front of their throat, lips closed, humming, with small buzz lines.
setup.caption: 1. Put two fingers on your throat and hum.

setup.art: A child with a hand resting flat on a purring grey cat's side, both looking calm.
setup.caption: 2. If a cat is near, rest a hand on her side as she purrs.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts two fingers gently on the front of their throat. 2. They hum 'mmmm' with lips closed, low like a big drum. 3. Then they hum high, like a whistle.
flow.say: Put your fingers on your throat. Hum low, mmmm. What do you feel? Now hum high. Is the buzz the same?
flow.kid: Fingers on your throat. Hum low. Now hum high. What do you feel?

ask.q: Which hum made a bigger buzz under your fingers?
good: The low hum buzzed more.
Both buzzed, but the low one felt stronger.

flow.parent: The low hum usually feels stronger. Your child is feeling their vocal folds vibrate inside the voice box. A cat's purr comes from her voice box too.

flow.do: Ask your child to hum while breathing out, then try to keep humming while breathing in.
flow.say: A cat purrs while she breathes in and while she breathes out. Can you hum while you breathe in? Try it.
flow.kid: Hum while you breathe out. Now try to hum while you breathe in. Is it hard?
flow.parent: Most people find humming while breathing in very hard, and it sounds strange. A purring cat keeps going through both breaths.

flow.do: If a cat lives with you, wait until she purrs on her own, then rest a hand gently on her side. If there is no cat, hum low again and rest your hand on your own chest, and skip the question.
flow.say: Can you feel the buzz in the cat's body? Is it faster or slower than your hum? When does she purr?
flow.kid: Rest your hand gently on the cat. Can you feel the purr?

ask.q: What do you think a purring cat is saying right now?
good: She is calm and likes being with us.
She wants us to stay close.

flow.parent: Never hold or squeeze a cat to make her purr. A purr is more than 20 vibrations every second, too fast to count.

activities.title: Messages Without a Voice: be a cricket and a woodpecker
activities.context: In this activity you make animal messages without using your voice: a cricket's chirp with a comb, a woodpecker's drumming with a pencil, and a touch message through a table.

materials.item: an old visiting card or a piece of thick card
a pencil and an empty cardboard box

schedule.what: Make a cricket chirp with a comb and card, drum like a woodpecker on a box, and send a knock message through a table.

activities.record: Draw the three messages you made and write who makes each one in nature.

setup.art: A child running the edge of a card along the teeth of a plastic comb, with small sound marks.
setup.caption: 1. Run a card along a comb: a cricket's chirp.

setup.art: A child with one ear pressed flat on a table while another child knocks gently on the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Press an ear to the table and feel a knock message.

flow.do: 1. Hold the comb still. 2. Run the edge of the card quickly along the comb's teeth. 3. Try fast and slow.
flow.say: A male cricket rubs one wing against the other. One wing has a row of tiny teeth, like this comb. Listen.
flow.kid: Run the card along the comb. Fast, then slow. You sound like a cricket!
flow.parent: A real cricket has a row of tiny ridges on one wing, called a file, and a scraper on the other. Female crickets hear the song with ears on their front legs.

flow.do: Your child drums the pencil on the box: first a slow knock-knock, then a very fast drum roll.
flow.say: Woodpeckers drum on wood with their beaks to say 'this is my place'. Drum on the box. Slow, then fast.
flow.kid: Drum on the box with the pencil. Slow, then very fast.
flow.parent: Woodpeckers drum on dead branches and even on metal poles, because these make a loud sound that carries far.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses one ear flat on the table and covers the other ear. 2. You knock gently at the far end: once, then three times, then a fast roll. 3. Swap.
flow.say: Ear on the table. Cover your other ear. How many knocks did you feel? Was it loud through the table?
flow.kid: Ear on the table. Count the knocks. Then swap.

ask.q: Was the knock louder through the table or through the air?
good: Through the table. It was much clearer.
Through the table, I could feel it.

flow.parent: Sound travels well through solid things. Some termites knock their heads on the walls of their tunnels to warn the others. The warning travels through the wood.

flow.do: Ask which message would work best in the dark, and which would work far away.
flow.say: Which of our messages would work in the dark? Which one could a friend hear far away?
flow.kid: Which message works in the dark? Which one goes far?

check.q: A cricket sings at night in a potted plant. Why is a sound a good message at night?
options: Sound works in the dark, when nobody can see a movement
Crickets cannot move in the day
check.why: In the dark, others cannot see a tail or a wing. But they can still hear a sound. That is one reason many night animals, like crickets and frogs, call loudly.

activities.title: Say Hello Like a Cat: the slow blink (if a cat is near)
activities.context: In this activity you try a cat's own way of saying 'I am friendly': a slow blink. You find out whether a cat blinks back. You need a cat who lives with you, or a calm cat at a friend's home.

materials.item: a calm cat who lives with you or a friend

activities.safety: Stay about two big steps away, and let the cat choose whether to come to you. Do not try this with a cat who is hiding, hissing or has her ears flat.

schedule.what: Sit near a calm cat. Look with a still face for a minute, then slow-blink for a minute, and note what she does each time.

activities.record: Write how many times the cat blinked slowly with a still face, and how many times after your slow blinks.

setup.art: A girl sitting on the floor about two steps from a grey cat on a mat, both looking at each other.
setup.caption: 1. Sit two steps from a calm cat.

setup.art: The girl with her eyes half closed in a slow blink, and the cat with her eyes half closed too.
setup.caption: 2. Narrow your eyes slowly, close them for a moment, then open.

flow.do: 1. Sit on the floor about two big steps from the cat. 2. For one minute, look at the cat with a still, plain face. 3. Count any slow blinks the cat makes.
flow.say: First, just look at the cat with a still face. Does she blink slowly? Let's count.
flow.kid: Sit still. Look at the cat. Count her slow blinks.
flow.parent: Do not stare hard. A hard stare can feel like a threat to a cat. A soft look is enough.

flow.do: For the next minute, slow-blink at the cat: narrow your eyes slowly, close them for about a second, then open them. Do it three or four times. Count the cat's slow blinks.
flow.say: Now let's say hello the cat way. Close your eyes slowly, then open them. Does she blink back?
flow.kid: Blink slowly at the cat. Does she blink back? Count.
flow.parent: In 2020, Tasmin Humphrey and Karen McComb tested this with cats in their homes. Cats slow-blinked more after people slow-blinked at them. They also came closer to a stranger who slow-blinked.

flow.do: Ask your child what happened and what it might mean.
flow.say: Did the cat blink more after your slow blinks? Did she come closer? What do you think she was saying?
flow.kid: Did she blink back? What was she saying, do you think?

ask.q: What might a cat's slow blink mean?
good: I feel safe with you.
Hello, I am friendly.

games.title: Who Said That? Act the sound, guess the message
games.context: This is an acting and guessing game. A player picks a card, makes the animal's sound or signal without saying who they are, and the others guess who is talking and what the message is.

setup.art: A pile of cards face down on a carpet, with a girl holding one card close to her chest so the others cannot see.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a card. Do not show anyone.

setup.art: The girl doing a play bow on the carpet, hands flat and bottom up, while two others shout guesses.
setup.caption: 2. Make the sound or the signal. The others guess who and what.

printables.title: 16 signal cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: A low, rough growl, with lips pulled back
items.b: A dog: 'Stay away from my food.'

items.f: High barks with gaps, and a play bow
Low, fast barks at the gate, no gaps
items.b: A dog: 'A stranger is here. Stay back.'

items.f: A soft, buzzing purr on a lap
items.b: A cat: 'I am calm. Stay close.'

items.f: A sharp hiss, back arched, fur puffed up
Walking towards someone with the tail straight up
A slow blink from across the room
items.b: A cat: 'I feel safe with you.'

items.f: 'Ku-oo! Ku-oo!', higher each time, from a tree

items.b: A female koel, with her own call.

items.f: Loud caws, and more crows flying in
items.b: Crows: 'Danger! A cat or an owl is here!'

items.f: A fast 'chip-chip-chip' and a flicking tail on a tree
A long, sweet song from a rooftop at dawn
items.b: A magpie robin: 'This is my place.'

items.f: Chirping all night by rubbing wings together
items.b: A male cricket: 'Here I am, come and find me.'
A mother hen: 'Come here, there is food.'

items.f: A loud cry, with a red face and fists
Fast drumming on a dead branch

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
The first player takes the top card and reads it silently. A grown-up can whisper it to a child who is not reading yet.
The player makes the sound or the signal. No real words, and no saying the animal's name.
The others guess who is talking, and what the message is. With 2 players, the other player guesses alone.

Turn the card over and read the back aloud. The actor scores 1 point if the animal is guessed, and 1 more point if the message is guessed. Keep the score on a sheet of paper, one column for each player.
Take turns until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins. If points are equal, everyone wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Mix them and make a pile, face down.
flow.say: Let's make the pile. The answer is on the back of each card, so don't peek.
flow.kid: Cut the cards. Mix them into a pile.

flow.do: Play rounds. Each player acts one card, and the others guess the animal and the message. Keep score on paper.
flow.say: Your turn. No words! Just the sound or the signal. Who are you, and what are you saying?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Make the sound. No words!

ask.q: Two cards were both dogs barking. How did you tell which message it was?
good: One was low and fast, for a stranger. The other was higher with gaps, for play.
The play one had a bow.

flow.parent: The hardest cards are the two dog barks, and the cat's raised tail and slow blink. Let the children argue it out. Arguing about what a signal means is exactly what animal scientists do.

flow.do: Ask which cards were easiest to guess, and why.
flow.say: Which cards were easiest to guess? Were they the low, rough ones or the high, soft ones?
flow.kid: Which ones were easy? Why?

check.q: A cat arches her back, puffs up her fur and hisses. What is her message?
check.why: Puffed-up fur makes a cat look bigger, and a hiss is a rough sound. Both say 'stay away'. If you picked 'stroke me', look again at the card: a friendly cat walks with her tail straight up.

games.title: Find My Chick: a voice game
games.context: King penguins live in huge crowds of thousands of birds. A parent coming back from the sea finds their own chick by the chick's voice. In this game a blindfolded 'parent' finds their 'chick' by a special call, while the other chicks call too.

setup.art: Three children each holding a small call card, while a woman ties a soft dupatta over her eyes like a blindfold.
setup.caption: 1. Each chick picks a call card. The parent is blindfolded.

setup.art: The blindfolded woman walking slowly with arms forward towards one child, while three children call different sounds around the room.
setup.caption: 2. All the chicks call at once. The parent walks to their own chick.

printables.title: 10 fish tokens to cut out and colour

rules: One player is the parent penguin. Everyone else is a chick. Use one call card for each chick.
Each chick picks one call card. One chick, chosen by the players, is the parent's own chick.
The parent's own chick says their call once in the parent's ear, so the parent learns it.
The parent puts on a soft blindfold, like a dupatta. A grown-up spins the parent gently once.
All the chicks stand around the room and say their own call again and again, at the same time.

The parent walks slowly with hands in front and listens, then touches one chick. If it is the parent's own chick, the parent takes a fish token. If not, that chick goes quiet, and the parent may try once more.
Swap roles. The game ends when everyone has been the parent twice. The player with the most fish wins. If it is a tie, the family shares the catch.
With only two players, the chick hides behind a sofa or a curtain and calls again and again. The parent finds the chick by the call.

flow.do: Tell the children how real king penguins find their chicks.
flow.say: King penguins live in crowds of thousands. When a parent comes back from the sea with fish, how do they find their own chick? By their voice!
flow.kid: Penguin parents find their chick by the chick's voice. Let's try.
flow.parent: Pierre Jouventin, Thierry Aubin and their team played recordings to king penguins on islands in the far south. Chicks answered their own parent's call and ignored other adults.

flow.do: Play several rounds, until everyone has been the parent twice. A grown-up keeps the space safe: move chairs and anything sharp out of the way first.
flow.say: Chicks, keep calling! Parent, listen hard. Which voice is your chick?
flow.kid: Keep saying your call. Parent, listen and find your chick.

ask.q: Parent, what helped you find the right chick?
good: I listened for the call I learned.
I walked to where that sound got louder.

flow.parent: It is harder than it sounds. Real penguin chicks also learn their parent's call and walk towards it. Both sides listen.

flow.do: Ask what made it hard and what made it easier.
flow.say: Was it hard with everyone calling? Would it be easier if every chick had the same call, or a different call?
flow.kid: Was it hard? Why does each chick need their own call?

check.q: Why does each penguin chick need their own call?
options: So their parent can pick them out from thousands of chicks
So they can sing louder than the sea
So other parents will feed them
check.why: In a crowd of thousands, a chick who sounded like everyone else could not be found. A call that is theirs alone lets the parent find them and bring them fish.

projects.title: Our Sound Dictionary: one animal, three days
projects.context: In this project you listen to one animal near your home for 5 minutes a day, for three days. Each time the animal makes a sound, you write what was happening. On day 3 you guess what each sound means. Scientists who study animal talk start exactly like this.

materials.item: a notebook with a page for each day
one animal you can hear from home: a crow, a pigeon, a street dog, a pet, a gecko on the wall or a koel

schedule.what: Choose an animal. Listen for 5 minutes. Write each sound and what was happening.
Listen to the same animal at about the same time. Add new sounds to the dictionary.
Listen again. Then guess what each sound means and write your guesses.

projects.record: A sound dictionary: one row for each sound, with how the sound goes, what was happening, a tally of how many times you heard it, and your guess of the message.

setup.art: A girl by a window grille with a notebook, listening to a crow cawing on the ledge of the next building.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal you can hear from home.

setup.art: A notebook page with three columns: a written sound like 'caw-caw-caw', a small drawing of what was happening, and a guess of the message.
setup.caption: 2. Write the sound, what was happening, and your guess.

flow.do: 1. Choose one animal you can hear from home. 2. Draw three columns: 'How the sound goes', 'What was happening', 'Guess of the message'. 3. Listen for 5 minutes. Write each sound the way it sounds, and what was happening.
flow.say: Let's be animal-talk scientists. Which animal shall we listen to? Each time they make a sound, what is going on?
flow.kid: Choose an animal. Listen. Write each sound and what was happening.
flow.parent: Crows and pigeons are around nearly every flat. At night, a gecko's 'tchk-tchk-tchk' on the wall works well. Write the sound in letters, like 'caw-caw' or 'grrr'. A child of this age can say it while you write.

flow.do: On day 2, listen to the same animal at about the same time, for 5 minutes. Add any new sounds. Make a tally mark when a sound comes again.
flow.say: Same animal, same time. Any new sounds today? Did an old sound come again? What was happening then?
flow.kid: Listen again. Is there a new sound? Make a tally for old ones.
flow.parent: If the same sound comes with the same thing happening, that is good evidence of its message. For example, loud caws every time a cat walks past.

flow.do: On day 3, listen once more. Then, for each sound, your child guesses the message and says why.
flow.say: Look at our dictionary. What do you think each sound means? What is your evidence?
flow.kid: What does each sound mean? Say why you think so.

ask.q: Which sound are you most sure about? Why?
good: The loud caw, because every time it came, a cat was on the wall.
The coo, because the pigeon cooed whenever another pigeon came close.

flow.parent: A guess backed by 'every time X happened, they made this sound' is real science. Scientists then test a guess by playing the sound back and watching.

challenges.title: Be a Tree Cricket: make a phone louder with no electricity
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In India, a small tree cricket chews a hole in a leaf, pushes his head through, and sings. The leaf makes his song louder. Can you make a phone's sound louder, the cricket's way, with only things from home?
challenges.problem: Can you make a phone's music reach farther across your flat using only paper, cups, tumblers or cardboard, with no extra speaker and no electricity?
constraints: Keep the phone at the same low loudness every time, so the sound fades away in a few steps.
Use only things from home: paper, a steel tumbler, a plastic cup, a bowl, a cardboard tube.
Do not cut or wet the phone. A grown-up handles any scissors.
Test by walking away from the phone until you can no longer hear the music. Count your steps.
materials: a steel tumbler or a bowl
a cardboard tube from a kitchen towel roll
general: Stand the phone upright in a steel tumbler or a bowl, with the speaker facing up.
Roll a sheet of newspaper into a cone and hold the narrow end over the phone's speaker.
creative: Cut a slot in the middle of a cardboard tube so the phone fits in tightly. Push a cup onto each end of the tube, facing outwards.
Cut a hole in a big leaf-shaped card, like the tree cricket's leaf. Hold the phone's speaker at the hole, so the card stands between the front and the back of the speaker.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own phone speaker. Count how many steps away you can still hear the music with no speaker, and then with your design. Change one thing and test again.

setup.art: A phone lying on a table playing music, and a child walking away counting steps, with numbers 1 to 8 on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Count how many steps away you can still hear the phone alone.

setup.art: The phone standing in a steel tumbler, and the child walking away again, counting steps.
setup.caption: 2. Put the phone in your design and count the steps again.

flow.do: Tell your child about the tree cricket. Read the problem together.
flow.say: A tree cricket chews a hole in a leaf and sings through it. The leaf makes his song much louder. Can we make a phone louder like that?
flow.kid: A tree cricket sings through a hole in a leaf. The leaf makes him louder. Can you do that for a phone?
flow.parent: This is real. Natasha Mhatre, Rohini Balakrishnan and their team studied tree crickets in India. In 2017 they showed that the leaf makes the male's song louder, and that the crickets pick leaves of a good size and make the hole in a good place.

flow.do: 1. Play music on the phone at the a low loudness. 2. Lay it on the table. 3. Your child walks away slowly, counting steps, until they cannot hear it. 4. Write the number.
flow.say: First, the phone alone. Walk away slowly. Stop when you can't hear the music. How many steps?
flow.kid: Walk away from the phone. Count your steps. Stop when you can't hear it.
flow.parent: Turn off the fan and close the windows if you can. Set the music low, so your child stops hearing it within a few steps. Keep the loudness the same for every test.

flow.do: Your child builds a design and tests it the same way. Try two or three designs.
flow.say: Now build your design. Will the tumbler, the cone or the tube work best? Why do you think so? Let's test.
flow.kid: Build a design. Put the phone in. Walk away and count again.

ask.q: Which design let you walk the most steps away?
good: The tumbler. I could hear it from the kitchen.
The tube with the cups, because the sound came out of both ends.

flow.parent: A tumbler, bowl or cone may make the music a little louder, because the hard sides send more of the sound the same way. The difference can be small. If you hear no difference, write that down. It is a real result, and another shape may do better.

flow.do: Ask why the designs worked, and link back to the cricket.
flow.say: Why do you think the tumbler or cone changed the music? Why might a cricket want to be loud?
flow.kid: Why was it louder? Why does a cricket want to be loud?

check.q: Why does a male tree cricket want his song to be loud?
options: So female crickets far away can hear him and come to him
So he can scare the leaf
So he does not have to eat
check.why: A louder song can be heard from farther away, so more female tree crickets can find him.

items.p: Draw a line from each sound to its message.
pairs: A cat's purr on a lap
Low, fast barks at the gate
A stranger is here. Stay back.
Loud caws, and more crows flying in
items.why: Each sound carries one message. A purr on a lap means calm and close. Low, fast barks warn a stranger. Loud caws call other crows to a danger. A koel's 'ku-oo' says 'I am here'.
items.art: Four pictures on the left, a purring cat, a barking dog, cawing crows and a koel, and four messages on the right.

items.p: A boy sees a dog give a low, rough growl over a bone. What is the dog most likely saying?
opts: This is my bone. Stay away.
items.why: A low, rough sound, often with lips pulled back, usually means 'stay away'. A play invitation sounds higher, with gaps, and comes with a play bow.
items.art: A brown dog lying with a bone between the front paws, lips pulled back, growling.

items.p: A dog's bark always means the same thing.
items.why: False. Low, rough, fast barks at a stranger mean 'stay back'. Higher barks with gaps, with a play bow, mean 'let's play'. The tune of the bark tells them apart.

items.p: Sort these messages: made with a sound, or made with the body?
items: a cat's tail held straight up
items.why: Purrs, barks and songs are sounds. A raised tail, a slow blink and a play bow are body signals, which others see instead of hear.

items.p: Remember the la-la test, where you said only 'la-la' from behind a door. Draw the message slip that your listener guessed right most often.
items.a: A drawing of one slip, for example the angry face with 'Go away!'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the message that got through best in your own test, often 'Go away!' or 'Help, I'm scared!'.
items.art: An empty box for drawing, shaped like a paper slip.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the la-la test, how did your listener know the message when you said no real words?
items.a: From the tune of my voice. 'Go away' was low and rough. 'Scared' was high and shaky.
items.why: A strong answer says that the word never changed, so the tune of the voice carried the message: high or low, rough or smooth.

items.p: Three of these send a message with a sound. Which one sends a message with the body?
opts: A cat walking with her tail straight up
items.why: A cat with her tail straight up is giving a body signal that means 'hello'. Barking, calling and purring are all sounds.

items.p: When a cat's voice box buzzes very fast while she breathes in and out, the sound is called a ________.
items.why: A purr is made by the voice box, more than 20 times every second, through both breaths.

items.p: Meera, aged 7, lives in Chennai. A street dog barks at her every morning at the gate of her building.

views.says: He sleeps at that gate. He is saying, 'This is my place.'
People feed him at the gate. Maybe he is asking you for food.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. What could Meera listen or look for, to find out?
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason, then says what to check: is the bark low and fast, or higher with gaps? Is his tail stiff or loose? Does he stop when she walks past, or follow her to where food is?
items.why: A bark can mean 'stay back', 'feed me' or 'let's play'. The tune of the bark and the dog's body help to tell them apart.

items.p: Rohan, a boy aged 5, says, 'Only people can talk. Animals just make noise.' Is he right? Say one thing from this unit that helps you answer.
items.a: He is not quite right. A dog barks differently at a stranger and in play, and the watchman comes. Vervet monkeys have a different call for each danger.
items.why: A strong answer uses one example where an animal's sound carries a message that others act on. It may also say that humans are animals too.

items.p: Which of these is a bird's song, not a call?
opts: A sharp 'chip!' as a cat comes near
A long tune sung again and again from the same rooftop every morning
A quick 'tik' as a bird flies off
items.why: A song is long and repeated, often from the same place, and says 'this is my place' or 'choose me'. Short single sounds, like 'chip' or 'tik', are calls.

items.p: In many kinds of songbirds, the females sing as well as the males.
items.why: True. In 2014 Karan Odom and her team found that in most of the kinds of songbirds they could check, females sing too.

items.p: Put these sounds in order, from the lowest pitch to the highest pitch.
items.why: Bigger bodies usually make lower sounds. A lion is the biggest here and a sparrow is the smallest.

items.p: Label the cat's body messages: tail straight up, fur puffed up, eyes half shut, ears flat back.
a: tail straight up: hello, I am friendly
fur puffed up: I am scared or angry, stay away
eyes half shut: I feel calm and safe
ears flat back: I am frightened or cross
items.why: A cat sends messages with her whole body. Read the tail, the fur, the eyes and the ears together.
items.art: Four small drawings of a cat, each with an empty label line: one with tail up, one with puffed fur, one with half-shut eyes and one with flat ears.

items.p: A kitten is born with her eyes and ears shut. How might her mother's purr help her in the first days? Say it, and a grown-up can write it.
items.a: The kitten can feel the buzz of the purr through her body, so she can find her mother and stay close, even before she can see or hear.
items.why: A strong answer says that a purr can be felt as well as heard, so it reaches a kitten who cannot yet see or hear. Scientists think this may help, but it is not fully shown.

items.p: Scientists hid a speaker in a bush and played a monkey's eagle alarm call, with no eagle there. Why did they use a speaker and no real eagle?
opts: So they knew the monkeys were reacting to the sound alone
items.why: With no eagle to see, only the call could tell the monkeys what to do. They looked up and hid in bushes, so the sound itself carried the message 'eagle'.

items.p: Draw two birds. One sings a song on a rooftop at dawn. The other gives a short alarm call at a cat. Show how the two sounds are different.
items.a: A bird with a long, wavy line of notes, and a bird with one short, sharp mark pointed at a cat.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the song as long and repeating, and the call as short and sharp, aimed at the danger.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to how they make their message.
pairs: rubs one wing against the other
drums on wood with the beak
speaks with the voice box, tongue and lips
items.why: A cricket's chirp comes from the wings, a woodpecker's drumming from the beak on wood, and a purr and human speech from the voice box.
items.art: A cricket, a woodpecker, a cat and a girl on the left, and four ways of making sound on the right.

items.p: Lakshmi and Farhan, two friends in Hyderabad, hear a male koel calling 'ku-oo, ku-oo' from a tree every morning.

views.says: He calls because he is happy.
He calls so that other koels know where he is. When a female is near, she can find him.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. What could they watch for, to find out?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then names a clue to watch: does the koel call more in the hot months, does another koel call back, or does a female come near?
items.why: We cannot know how a koel feels, but we can watch what happens after the call. A call that others answer is a message.

items.p: A short sound that warns others that danger is near is called an ________ call.
items.why: An alarm call warns others of danger, like a crow's loud caws at a cat or a squirrel's fast 'chip-chip-chip'.

items.p: Many animals use low, rough sounds to say 'stay away'. Why might a low sound help an animal look stronger?
items.a: Big animals and big drums make low sounds. So a low growl makes an animal sound bigger than they are, and others keep away.
items.why: A strong answer links low pitch with big size: bigger bodies make deeper sounds, so a low sound is a way of sounding big.

items.p: Sita is doing the la-la test. She makes her 'Go away!' la-la high and squeaky. What will the listener most likely guess?
opts: The listener will always get it right anyway
items.why: High, shaky sounds usually mean fear or 'help'. A 'go away' message is usually low and rough. So the listener will probably guess 'scared'.

items.p: Two people argue about whether animal calls are like words.

views.says: Animal calls show feelings, like a cry of fear. Only people have real words.

views.who: Dorothy Cheney, who studied vervet monkeys in Kenya
views.says: Vervets have a different alarm call for a leopard, an eagle and a snake. Each call tells the others which danger is near, so they know where to hide.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, such as the vervets running up trees only at the leopard call. Then it gives the other side its due: people can say endless new things, and no monkey has been shown to do that.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Vervet calls name the kind of danger, which is a bit like a word. But human language puts words together in endless new ways.

items.p: A pet cat meows at people a lot. Scientists have noticed that grown-up cats rarely meow at each other. Who do you think the meow is for? Why?
items.a: The meow is mostly for people. Cats may have learned that meowing gets people to open doors or give food.
items.why: A strong answer uses the clue that cats meow far more at people than at cats, and says what the cat might be asking for.

items.p: A wagging tail always means a dog is friendly.
items.why: False. Dogs also wag when excited, unsure or ready to snap. A stiff tail held high and wagging fast in small movements can be a warning. Look at the whole dog.

items.p: Invent an animal who lives in a dark cave. Draw how they tell the others 'food is here!'. Will it be a sound, a touch or both? Write why.
items.a: For example, a cave animal who clicks loudly and taps the ground, because in the dark nobody can see a body signal.
items.why: A strong design uses a signal that works in the dark, such as a sound or a touch, and says why a body signal like a raised tail would not work there.

items.p: Which messages still work in the dark?
items: a cat's tail held straight up
a mother cat's purr against her kittens
a peacock spreading his tail feathers
items.why: Sounds and touch work in the dark. Body signals, like a raised tail or a spread of feathers, must be seen, so they need light.

items.p: A small tree cricket chews a hole in a leaf and sings with his head pushed through the hole. Why?
opts: The leaf makes his song louder
To eat the leaf while he sings
items.why: The leaf stops the sound from the front and the back of his wings from cancelling each other out. So the song is much louder and can be heard from farther away.

items.p: In the la-la test, why were the slips mixed in a bowl before the sender picked one?
opts: So the listener could not guess the order of the messages
So the slips would not get lost
So the sender could read them more easily
items.why: If the slips were in a fixed order, the listener could guess the next message without listening to the tune. Mixing them makes the test fair.

items.p: A mother hen clucks, and her chicks run to her. Who is the sender? What is the signal? Who is the receiver? Say it, and a grown-up can write it.
items.a: The hen is the sender. The cluck is the signal. The chicks are the receivers, because they notice it and run to her.
items.why: A strong answer names all three and says that the receiver does something because of the signal.

quiz.p: What does it mean when an animal communicates?
opts: They send a message, and another animal notices and acts on the message.
They make a noise by accident.
quiz.why: Communicating needs a sender and a receiver. The signal changes what the receiver does, like crows flying up at an alarm call.

quiz.p: Which of these is a message sent with the body, not with a sound?
opts: A dog doing a play bow, front legs down and back end up
quiz.why: A play bow is a body signal that others see. Purring and cawing are sounds.

quiz.p: How does a cat make a purr?
opts: Her voice box vibrates very fast as she breathes in and out
quiz.why: A purr comes from the voice box, more than 20 times every second, through both breaths. That is why you can feel it.

quiz.p: A cat is purring while her paw is hurt. What does this tell you?
opts: A purr can mean more than 'I am happy'.
The cat is happy to be hurt.
quiz.why: Cats purr when hurt or frightened too. You read a purr with the rest of the cat and with what is happening.

quiz.p: Which sound is a bird's alarm call?
opts: A long tune at sunrise from a rooftop
A sharp, loud cry when a cat comes near the nest
A loud 'ku-oo' again and again from a tree
quiz.why: An alarm call is short and sharp and warns of danger. A long tune is a song, and 'ku-oo' is a koel's call to say 'I am here'.

quiz.p: In many kinds of songbirds, who sings?
quiz.why: In most kinds of songbirds that scientists checked, females sing as well as males.

quiz.p: A cat puffs up her fur and hisses with a rough sound. What is she most likely saying?
quiz.why: Rough sounds and a puffed-up body usually mean 'stay away'. Puffed fur also makes her look bigger.

quiz.p: Which kind of sound more often means 'I am friendly' or 'help me'?
opts: Any sound, it makes no difference
quiz.why: In many birds and mammals, high, soft sounds go with being friendly or scared, and low, rough sounds go with 'stay away'.

quiz.p: A male cricket chirps all night in a potted plant. How does he make the sound?
opts: By rubbing one wing against the other
quiz.why: One wing has a row of tiny ridges and the other has a scraper. Rubbing them together makes the chirp.

quiz.p: In the la-la test, why did the sender hide behind a door?
opts: So the listener could not see the face or hands, and only the sound could help
So the sound would be louder
So the sender could read the slips more easily
quiz.why: A face can give the answer away. Hiding makes sure the test is only about the sound.

quiz.p: Your listener got 10 out of 12 right in the la-la test. What does this show?
opts: The tune of a sound can carry a message, even with no words.
quiz.why: The word never changed and the sender was hidden, so the tune carried the message. Guessing alone would give only about 3 right out of 12.

applications: Vets and animal shelter workers read barks, purrs, tails and ears to tell whether an animal is in pain or frightened.
Bird scientists count birds in forests by their songs and calls, often with microphones left in the trees for days.
People who train guide dogs and police dogs use the tune of their voice as much as their words.
Farmers who keep hens and cows learn their animals' calls, and can hear when a hen has seen a hawk or a calf is hungry.

open_questions.q: Why do cats purr when they are hurt?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think the purr calms the cat. Some think the buzz might help the body heal. Nobody has shown which is true.

open_questions.q: Do any animals have words, or a language like ours?
open_questions.why_open: Some monkeys and birds have calls for different dangers, and some put calls in a set order. Scientists still argue about whether this is like human language.

open_questions.q: How much of what a dog's bark says is meant for people?
open_questions.why_open: Dogs bark far more than wolves do. Scientists think that dogs may have come to bark more while living with people, but nobody is sure how much of the barking is for us.

maths.problem: In the story, Rohan, a boy aged 5, listened in the la-la test. He got 3 right for 'Go away!', 2 for 'Come here!', 2 for 'I am happy' and 2 for 'Help, I'm scared!'. How many did he get right in all, out of 12? How many were wrong?
maths.explain: 3 and 2 make 5. 5 and 2 make 7. 7 and 2 make 9. There were 12 tries, and 12 take away 9 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the la-la test, where one person sends messages from behind a door using only 'la-la'.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the tallies for each message shows how well the tune carried the messages.

maths.problem: There were 4 kinds of message and 12 tries. If Rohan had covered his ears and only guessed, about how many would he get right? He got 9. How many times more is that?
maths.answer: About 3 by guessing. 9 is 3 times as many as 3.
maths.explain: A pure guess is right about 1 time in 4. 12 shared into 4 equal groups is 3. 3 and 3 and 3 make 9, so 9 is three times 3.
maths.context: This is about the la-la test, and whether the listener was just lucky.
maths.why_maths: Working out what luck alone would give tells us whether the result really means something.

maths.problem: A cat purrs about 25 buzzes every second. How many buzzes in 4 seconds?
maths.explain: 4 groups of 25. 25 and 25 make 50. 50 and 50 make 100.
maths.context: This is about the purr, which is too fast to count, as in the Hum a Purr activity.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups shows how fast a purr is, even though we cannot count it by ear.

maths.problem: In her sound dictionary, Ayesha, a girl in Class 2, heard the crow caw 14 times, the pigeon coo 6 times and the street dog bark 9 times. Put the animals in order, from most sounds to fewest. How many more caws than coos?
maths.answer: Crow 14, dog 9, pigeon 6. There were 8 more caws than coos.
maths.explain: 14 is more than 9, and 9 is more than 6. Count on from 6 to 14: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. That is 8 more.
maths.context: This is about the sound dictionary project, where you listen to one animal for three days.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order shows at a glance which animal talked the most.

maths.problem: A cricket chirps in a pattern: chirp, chirp, rest, chirp, chirp, rest. What comes after the third rest? If the pattern goes round 5 times, how many chirps is that?
maths.answer: Chirp comes next. 5 rounds make 10 chirps.
maths.explain: Each round is chirp, chirp, rest, so it has 2 chirps. 5 rounds of 2 chirps: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
maths.context: This is about crickets, who chirp in patterns at night.
maths.why_maths: Many animal calls repeat in patterns. Finding the pattern helps you tell one animal's call from another's.

roots.context: We have listened to barks, purrs and birdsong, and sent messages with only 'la-la'. Now we ask what the la-la test tells us about ourselves and other animals.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, the listener guessed 'go away' or 'scared' from a sound with no words. Dogs, cats and people all make low, rough sounds to warn others off. High, soft sounds often mean 'I am friendly' or 'help me'. So the tune of a sound carries a message that many kinds of animals understand.
deep_truth.habit: We think a message lives in its words, so animals without words have nothing to say. But in your test the word never changed, and the message still got through.
deep_truth.evidence: In the la-la test, the listener got far more right than guessing alone would give. In 1977 Eugene Morton found that many birds and mammals use low, rough sounds to threaten and high, clear sounds when friendly or afraid. In 2017 Piera Filippi and her team found that people can hear whether frogs, alligators, pandas and elephants are calm or excited.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who talks with words, and also with the tune of your voice. A dog notices your tune as well as your words.
three.what_is_life: Living beings send messages all the time: to warn, to call, to ask for food, and to say 'I am here'.
three.what_is_this_world: The air around a flat is full of messages: barks, caws, chirps and purrs, each one meant for someone.

roots.thread: Every message needs two beings: one who sends and one who receives. A crow's alarm call works only when another crow hears and flies up. A purr is felt by the kitten pressed against her mother. So a message lives between two beings, not inside one. Each kind of animal speaks in their own way, and yet a dog's growl and an angry human voice share the same low, rough tune.

teachings.teaching: Just as a crystal shows the colour of whatever is beside it, the face shows what the heart is feeling strongly.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar wrote about reading feelings without words. In the la-la test the face was hidden, yet the voice still showed what the sender felt, the way a dog's growl or a cat's hiss does.

teachings.teaching: Solomon says, 'O people, we have been taught the language of the birds.'
teachings.link: This old teaching treats birds as beings with a language worth learning. Scientists who record calls and play them back are trying to learn that language, one call at a time.

science.text: Vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and act on each call even when no danger is there.
Whether any animal other than humans has words, or a language like ours, is still argued about.

other_view.who: Many scientists who study language, such as Noam Chomsky
other_view.view: They say animal sounds are signals, not language. A call can say 'danger', but animals do not put sounds together to say endless new things, as people do with words. Some scientists also think many animal calls simply burst out with a feeling, the way you shout 'ow!', and are not chosen.

how_we_found_out.story: Until the 1970s, many scientists thought animal calls were only cries of feeling, like a scream of fear. They did not think a call could tell others what kind of danger it was. In Amboseli, in Kenya, vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes. Thomas Struhsaker had noticed this in the 1960s. Dorothy Cheney, Robert Seyfarth and Peter Marler wanted to test whether the sound alone carried the message. They recorded the calls. Then they hid a loudspeaker in a bush and played a call when no danger was there. At the leopard call, the monkeys ran up into the trees. At the eagle call, they looked up at the sky or ran into bushes. At the snake call, they stood up on their back legs and looked down at the grass. So each call told the others which danger was near. They published this in 1980.
how_we_found_out.who: Dorothy Cheney and Robert Seyfarth, American scientists, with Peter Marler, after Thomas Struhsaker first noticed the calls
how_we_found_out.when: Struhsaker described the calls in 1967. Cheney, Seyfarth and Marler published their speaker tests in 1980.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That animal calls are only cries of feeling and cannot tell others about the world. The hidden-speaker tests showed that each vervet call tells the others which danger is near.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman crouching in tall dry grass in Kenya beside a small hidden loudspeaker, watching vervet monkeys run up an acacia tree.
